title: C. R. Klewin, Inc. v. Flagship Properties, Inc.
lead: A developer allegedly promised a construction company the management of a vast project without specifying its duration. Connecticut held that expected years of work did not bring that oral promise within the one-year statute of frauds when its terms prescribed no such duration.

actors.name: C. R. Klewin, Inc.
actors.role: Construction company claiming a project-wide management agreement

proceedings: Federal district court granted summary judgment under the one-year statute of frauds; Second Circuit certified state-law questions; Connecticut Supreme Court answered yes to the first and no to the second, without deciding ultimate contract liability.
limits: The supplied source reserves formation and contractual definiteness. This account transforms that brief and supplies no independent opinion audit or current-treatment certification.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A handshake for a large development
paragraphs: Flagship Properties and DKM Properties, operating together as Conn-Tech, planned a $120 million development near the University of Connecticut’s Mansfield campus. It included twenty industrial buildings, a 280-room hotel and convention center, and housing for 592 graduate students and professors.

At a March 1986 dinner, representatives discussed hiring C. R. Klewin, Inc., a provider of construction and construction-management services, as construction manager. Klewin proposed four percent of construction cost plus four percent for overhead and profit, subject to adjustment for the timing of project phases. Flagship’s representative ended with a handshake and an assurance that Klewin had the job and they had a deal.

The parties publicized the arrangement, held a videotaped press conference, and ceremonially signed an American Institute of Architects form with its blanks unfilled. No detailed project-wide written agreement followed. The facts presented later did not conclusively establish other specific terms, particularly an express completion time.

sections.title: The developer changes contractors after the first phase
paragraphs: The parties separately signed a written agreement for the first phase, Celeron Square. Work began May 4, 1987, and finished by mid-October. By then, Flagship was dissatisfied with Klewin’s work and discussing other contractors. In March 1988, it hired another contractor for sitework on Celeron Square II.

Klewin maintained that the original oral agreement covered construction management for the entire development. It sued in the federal District of Connecticut for breach, quantum meruit for services anticipating later phases, and detrimental reliance on a promise to pay for preconstruction work.

sections.title: The federal courts ask what the one-year rule requires
paragraphs: Flagship sought summary judgment, arguing among other things that the oral agreement violated Connecticut’s one-year statute of frauds. General Statutes § 52-550(a)(5) required a signed writing for an agreement not to be performed within one year of its making.

The district court accepted that defense. It reasoned that an undertaking ending upon project completion was not indefinite and that this project could not possibly be finished in a year. Klewin had acknowledged an intended construction period of three to ten years.

On appeal, the Second Circuit found no clearly controlling Connecticut precedent. It certified whether an agreement stating no performance time is indefinite and outside the provision, and whether the provision bars an agreement whose performance contemplates more than a year but whose terms do not expressly exclude earlier completion. The Connecticut Supreme Court accepted those questions under its certification jurisdiction.

sections.title: Connecticut focuses on the promised terms
paragraphs: Chief Justice Peters, writing for a unanimous five-member court, chose a narrow reading. The statute descended from the 1677 English law addressing fraud and perjury, but its one-year clause poorly tracked modern evidentiary concerns. It measured neither the interval before litigation nor the size of an undertaking: immediate suit could be barred while memories remained fresh, and one day’s work scheduled thirteen months away could fall within the clause while a full year’s work beginning immediately did not.

Those concerns did not repeal the statute or erase an express multi-year term. They counseled against expanding it through a factual inquiry into practical completion time. Connecticut decisions consistently focused on what the agreement required. Russell v. Slade demanded that inability to perform within a year appear from the agreement; Clark v. Pendleton distinguished an expected eighteen-month voyage from a contractual duration. Appleby and Burkle likewise examined terms precluding performance, while Finley rejected actual duration and parties’ probability estimates as controlling.

Repeated legislative reenactment of similar wording supported that interpretation. An identifiable endpoint, such as a completed development, did not itself prescribe when that endpoint must occur. The relevant possibility was consistency with contractual terms, rather than realistic feasibility.

sections.title: The court confronts contrary arguments and examples
sections.cue: Why scale does not change the answer
paragraphs: Flagship argued that one-year performance must be reasonably possible. It invoked Burkle, which refused to remove a partnership obligation from the statute merely because all partners might die within a year. Peters explained that refusing to extend a death-contingency exception did not alter the terms-based rule. Burkle involved an obligation understood as permanent or perpetual, even though described there as indefinite; perpetual and unspecified durations were different.

The court also relied on Warner v. Texas & Pacific Railway, where a rail switch was expected to remain useful for many years but no contractual term required that duration. Both expected and actual longevity left that agreement outside the provision.

The court acknowledged a contrary Restatement illustration treating a promise to sell five Minnesota potato crops as within the statute because five crops could not mature in one year. That approach considered the realistic nature of performance. Connecticut instead preferred the Restatement’s Warner-based illustration and its own restrictive rule. Litigating the practical feasibility of an unspecified completion period would consume resources without deciding formation, breach, or the underlying merits.

sections.title: Answers return to the federal appeal
paragraphs: The Connecticut Supreme Court answered the first certified question yes and the second no, taxing neither party costs. An oral agreement without an express duration beyond one year was functionally an indefinite-duration agreement for this provision, regardless of actual performance time. Judges Shea, Glass, Covello, and Berdon joined without separate writings.

The answer defeated the particular statutory reasoning based on the project’s expected three-to-ten-year schedule. It did not establish that the handshake formed a sufficiently definite contract, that the blank signed form satisfied other writing requirements, or that Flagship owed the contemplated management fee. The state court returned legal answers to the federal appeal rather than entering a damages judgment.
